title: The Queer Nonverbal Dialect
hook: “Gaydar” feels like reading; the research says it mostly measures stereotypes, and acting on it can out someone who never chose to be seen.
why:
Most men have, at some point, looked at another man and wondered whether he was gay. Popular culture calls the supposed ability to tell gaydar, and many people believe they have it. This chapter is partly about whether that belief holds up, and mostly about what to do instead of acting on it.

Gay, bisexual and other queer men do have their own nonverbal dialect: ways of signalling to each other, of testing whether it is safe to be open, of showing interest or affection under conditions where being misread can be dangerous. That dialect deserves understanding and respect. But it is not a code for outsiders to crack. The more useful skill, for most readers, is knowing when not to read at all.

This chapter covers what the research on gaydar actually found, why lab accuracy collapses in the real world, what guessing costs the people guessed about, how the dialect works and why it is so often deliberately ambiguous, attraction between men, which the chapter on attraction in Part III promised to return to, and how to be a reader in whose company people feel safe.

teach.h: Why this chapter is mostly about not reading.
teach.p:
Every other chapter in this book teaches you to notice more. This one asks you to notice something and then put it down. Sexual orientation is not a behaviour, a mood or an intention. It is part of who someone is, and whether to share it, with whom and when, is entirely their decision.

The temptation to read it anyway is strong, and it usually comes from curiosity rather than malice. But a reading of orientation is not like a reading of tiredness or tension. If you are wrong, you have attached a label to someone that may follow them. If you are right and you act on it, by asking, hinting, telling others or treating them differently, you have taken a decision that was theirs to make.

In many workplaces and families this decision still carries real risk. In some countries same-sex relationships remain illegal. Even in more accepting places, many people choose carefully whom to tell, and when. Being guessed about removes that choice.

So the discipline of this chapter is restraint. Notice that you are wondering, recognise that it is not your question to answer, and return to reading the person in front of you as an individual: their mood, their comfort, their wish to talk or be left alone. The figure here stands at rest. Nothing about how he stands tells you whom he loves, and nothing needs to.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if guessing at someone's orientation carried no risk for them. People who are outed without their consent describe loss of control over a deeply personal decision, and in some places guessing can expose people to danger.

teach.p:
Psychologists have tested gaydar directly. In 2008 Nicholas Rule and Nalini Ambady showed observers photographs of men's faces, taken from dating profiles, for as little as a twentieth of a second, and asked them to judge whether each man was gay or straight. Observers did better than chance, but not by much: in the briefest condition, they were right roughly 57 per cent of the time, where guessing would give 50.

In 2007 Kerri Johnson and her colleagues studied body movement. Observers watched animated figures and filmed people walking, and judged their orientation. They relied heavily on gender stereotypes: men who walked with a sway of the hips, rather than a swagger of the shoulders, were judged gay. With real walkers, observers were right somewhat more than 60 per cent of the time for men, and no better than chance for women.

These findings are often reported as proof that gaydar is real. A more careful reading is that, in a laboratory, with a set of photographs or walkers in which half are gay, people do slightly better than a coin toss, mostly by using stereotypes about gender.

That is a modest result, and the next block shows why it shrinks almost to nothing outside the lab. The figure here walks with an ordinary stride. Observers in these studies would have been confident about him, one way or the other, and often wrong.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if observers judged orientation from faces or walks with high accuracy. In these studies, accuracy was only modestly above chance, and largely driven by gender stereotypes.

teach.h: Why lab accuracy fails on the street.
teach.p:
In most laboratory studies, about half the people shown are gay. In real life the proportion is far smaller: surveys in many countries put the share of people who identify as gay or lesbian at a few per cent. This matters enormously.

Suppose you could tell gay from straight men with 60 per cent accuracy, better than most studies found. In a room of a hundred men where five are gay, you would correctly pick out three of the five. But you would also wrongly label about thirty-eight of the ninety-five straight men as gay. Most of your gay guesses would be wrong. Researchers call this the false positive paradox.

In 2016 William Cox, Janet Hyde and their colleagues went further. They found that the apparent accuracy of judgments from faces could be explained by differences in the photographs, such as image quality, rather than anything about the faces. They also found that people readily inferred orientation from stereotypes about fashion, interests and jobs. And when participants were told that gaydar was real, they stereotyped more.

The researchers concluded that gaydar works less as a skill than as a licence to stereotype. Believing in it makes people more willing to apply assumptions about how gay men look and behave, and those assumptions are wrong about most people. The figure here sits with his chin on his hand, thinking. Thinking carefully about this question leads to the conclusion that it cannot be answered by looking.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if real-world guesses about orientation were mostly correct. Because gay people are a small minority, even modest lab accuracy produces mostly wrong guesses in everyday life.
teach.pullQuote: Gaydar works less as a skill than as a licence to stereotype.

teach.p:
Speculating about whether a colleague, a friend or a relative is gay can feel harmless, even affectionate. It rarely is.

Being the subject of speculation is uncomfortable for anyone. For someone who is gay and has not told people, it creates a choice they did not want: deny it, confirm it on someone else's timetable, or live with the gossip. For someone who is straight, it attaches a label based on how they walk, speak or dress, which often means it attaches to men who do not fit narrow ideas of masculinity. Boys and men who are gentle, artistic or uninterested in sport have long been targeted with exactly these guesses.

Speculation also tells the people around you something about you. A gay colleague who hears others guessing about someone else learns that this is a place where people are watched and discussed. That is information they will use when deciding whether to be open.

The practical rule is simple. Do not speculate aloud, do not join in when others do, and do not ask someone directly whether they are gay unless you have a real reason and a relationship that can bear it. If someone wants you to know, they will tell you. The figures here stand in a small group, the kind of circle in which a careless guess about someone outside it travels fast.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if speculation about orientation had no effect on the people speculated about or those who overheard it. Gay men's accounts of choosing whether to come out at work and in families consistently describe weighing how others talk about people like them.

teach.p:
Queer men do have nonverbal ways of recognising and signalling to one another, and they are worth understanding, not so that outsiders can decode them, but so that they can understand why they work as they do.

Because being openly gay has often been dangerous, many of these signals are deliberately ambiguous. A glance held a beat longer than usual. A reference to a partner without a gender. A mention of a bar, a film or a neighbourhood that means something to those who know. Each of these can be read by someone who shares the dialect and passed over by someone who does not, which is the point. They allow people to find each other while keeping deniability if the reading turns out to be wrong, or the person turns out to be hostile.

This is a familiar pattern in any group that has needed to be careful: signals designed to be read by insiders and missed by everyone else. The next chapter looks at how the same need for safety shapes what couples do in public.

For a reader who is not part of the dialect, two lessons follow. First, ambiguity is often deliberate, and resolving it by asking or guessing defeats its purpose. Second, if someone does use a gender-neutral word for their partner, follow their lead and use it too until they choose otherwise. The figure here tilts his head, listening. Some things said to him will carry a second layer of meaning, intended for someone else.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if the signals queer men use to find each other were mostly unambiguous. Their deliberate ambiguity, allowing deniability, reflects the risks that openness has carried.

teach.p:
The chapter on attraction in Part III dealt mainly with men reading women, and promised to return to attraction between men. The core of that chapter applies unchanged. Interest shows mainly as attention: turning toward someone, staying close, asking questions, touching briefly, holding a gaze. Men tend to overread interest. Friendliness is not desire. The only reliable reading is a clear answer to a question, and no means no.

Between men, there is an added layer of uncertainty. Neither person may know whether the other is gay or bisexual, and getting it wrong can be embarrassing or, with a hostile person, dangerous. So signals of interest are often subtler and more deniable, and they are tested gradually, as the previous block described.

Two kinds of misreading follow. A gay or bisexual man may read friendliness from a straight man as interest. A straight man may read ordinary warmth from a gay man as a pass, and react with discomfort or hostility. The chapters on the bro hug and on space between men in Part III described how the fear of seeming gay has shaped how straight men touch and stand. That fear, which researchers have called homohysteria, has eased in many places but not disappeared.

The response is the same as with anyone. If you are interested, ask, with room for no. If you are not, say so kindly and clearly, as you would to a woman, without contempt. The figures here stand at an angle, close enough to talk and far enough that either can step away: the right distance for a question.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if attraction between men followed entirely different rules from attraction in general. The same signals and the same hard limits apply; the added uncertainty about orientation and safety mainly makes signals subtler.

teach.p:
For most readers of this book, the most useful thing to learn about queer body language is how their own body language is read by queer people.

When a same-sex couple holds hands in the street or kisses goodbye at a station, respond exactly as you would to any couple, which usually means not responding at all. A stare, a double take or a nudge to a friend is noticed, and remembered. When a colleague mentions a husband or a boyfriend, ask about their weekend in the same tone you would use with anyone. Surprise, even friendly surprise, tells them they were not what you expected.

Use neutral words, such as partner, until you are told otherwise. Do not assume that the man in front of you is straight, or that his wife is the person he lives with. When others make jokes or guesses about someone's orientation, a quiet change of subject, or a plain Leave it, does more than you might think.

None of this requires you to understand the queer dialect. It requires you to make your own body language easy to read: relaxed, unsurprised, interested in the person rather than the category. The figures here are two men walking hand in hand. The most helpful thing a passer-by can do is nothing at all.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if the reactions of passers-by and colleagues made no difference to whether gay people felt safe being open. Gay men consistently describe reading the room for exactly these reactions before deciding how open to be.

caseStudy:
Matt, twenty-nine, works in a sales team of eight men. A new colleague, Dan, joined in the spring: friendly, well dressed, uninterested in football. Within a fortnight, two of the others had decided he was gay, and the guessing had become a running joke when Dan was out of the room. Matt laughed along, though it made him slightly uncomfortable.

One afternoon Dan came back to his desk earlier than expected and caught the end of a joke. Nobody said anything. Dan went quiet for the rest of the day and ate lunch alone for the next week.

Matt thought about it that evening. He realised he had no idea whether Dan was gay, that it was none of his business, and that the joke had told Dan something about the team whichever way it went. The next time it started, he said, quietly, Leave it, he's a good bloke. The others shrugged, and it stopped.

A few months later, at a team dinner, Dan mentioned his husband in passing, testing the water. Matt asked what his husband did for a living and how long they had been together, exactly as he would have with anyone. Dan relaxed visibly. Later he told Matt he had been close to leaving the job in the spring, and that the change in the office had been the reason he stayed. Matt had not thought of two words, Leave it, as a decision that might keep someone in a job. He thought about it often afterwards.
observe: Notice any moment this week when you wonder about someone's orientation, and practise putting the question down.
Notice how people around you react to same-sex couples in public, and what those reactions would tell a gay man watching.
Notice the words you use for people's partners, and whether you assume a gender before you are told.
Notice jokes or guesses about someone's orientation, and how the people present respond.

drills.name: Put the Question Down
steps: The next time you find yourself wondering whether someone is gay, notice it.
Ask yourself what you would do with the answer if you had it.
Recognise that the question is theirs to answer, not yours.
Return your attention to something you can actually read: their mood, comfort or wish to talk.

drills.name: Neutral by Default
steps: For one week, use partner rather than wife or girlfriend when asking about someone's life, until they tell you more.
Notice how often you would otherwise have assumed.
When someone tells you about their partner, mirror the words they use.
Note any moment where the neutral word made a conversation easier.

drills.name: The Quiet Interruption
steps: Prepare one short line you could use to end speculation about someone's orientation, such as Leave it, it's his business.
Practise saying it in a calm, ordinary tone.
The next time speculation starts, use it.
Afterwards, note how the group responded.

drills.name: Unremarkable
steps: The next time you see a same-sex couple showing affection in public, notice your first reaction.
Practise letting your face and body stay exactly as they would for any couple.
Reflect on what a stare or a double take would have communicated.
Write one sentence about what you noticed in yourself.

quiz.q: A friend says he can always tell who is gay just by looking. What does the research suggest?
options: He is right, since lab studies show people judge orientation from faces with very high accuracy
Lab accuracy is only slightly above chance, and in real life most such guesses would be wrong
Nobody can ever do better than chance, so the studies all found exactly fifty per cent accuracy
Only gay men can tell, because they share the same signals and nobody else can read them
quiz.explain: Observers in lab studies do only modestly better than chance. Because gay people are a small minority, even that accuracy produces mostly wrong guesses in everyday life.

quiz.q: In Rule and Ambady's 2008 study, how accurate were observers who saw men's faces for a twentieth of a second?
options: About 57 per cent, where guessing would give 50
About 95 per cent, close to perfect accuracy
Exactly 50 per cent, no better than guessing
About 30 per cent, worse than random guessing
quiz.explain: Observers did slightly better than chance in the laboratory. Later work questioned whether even that came from the faces or from differences in the photographs.

quiz.q: What did Johnson and colleagues find observers relied on when judging orientation from how people walked?
options: The length of each stride, which observers measured very precisely
The speed of walking, with faster walkers judged straight every time
Gender stereotypes, judging hip sway in men as a sign of being gay
Nothing in particular, since observers guessed entirely at random
quiz.explain: Observers linked gender-atypical movement, such as hip sway in men, to being gay. Accuracy with real walkers was modestly above chance for men and at chance for women.

quiz.q: What did Cox and colleagues find when they told participants that gaydar was real?
options: Participants became more accurate at judging orientation from faces alone
Participants refused to make any judgments about orientation at all
Participants judged everyone to be straight, whatever they were shown
Participants relied more on stereotypes when judging orientation
quiz.explain: Believing in gaydar made people more willing to apply stereotypes. The researchers concluded that gaydar works more as a licence to stereotype than as a skill.

quiz.q: A colleague mentions in passing that he and his husband went walking at the weekend. What fits this chapter best?
options: Ask where they walked and how long they have been together, as you would anyone
Say you had no idea he was gay, so that he knows you are fine with it
Change the subject quickly, so that neither of you feels uncomfortable
Tell the rest of the team afterwards, so they know not to make jokes
quiz.explain: Responding in the same tone you would use with anyone tells him that this is unremarkable. Surprise, even friendly surprise, signals that he was not what you expected.

quiz.q: At a bar, a man you do not know holds your gaze and comes over to talk. You are not interested. What fits this chapter best?
options: Make it clear you find the idea offensive, so he does not try again
Be friendly and say plainly that you are not interested, as with anyone
Ignore him completely and turn your back until he goes away again
Play along to avoid awkwardness, then leave when he goes to the bar
quiz.explain: The same principles apply as with any approach: a clear, kind answer, without contempt. Hostility to a gay man's interest is a reaction to the category, not to anything he did.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific time you wondered about, guessed at or joked about someone's sexual orientation, or heard others do so. Describe what prompted the guess: a way of walking, talking, dressing or not fitting in. What would you have done with the answer? Now imagine you were that person and had overheard. What would it have told you about the people around you? Describe one thing you will do differently the next time the subject comes up.
reflection.guidance: Most men have done this, usually without malice. The point is not guilt but awareness of what guessing costs and communicates. Be specific about the moment and about the alternative: putting the question down, using neutral words, or quietly ending the speculation.

failureMode: The first failure is to believe you can tell someone's orientation by looking, when lab accuracy is barely above chance and real-world guesses are mostly wrong. The second is to speculate aloud or join in when others do, which can out people and tells everyone listening whether it is safe to be open. The third is to ask someone directly when you have no real reason. The fourth is to try to decode the deliberately ambiguous signals queer men use with each other. The fifth is to react to a same-sex couple, or to a colleague's mention of a husband, with visible surprise. And the sixth is to answer a man's interest with contempt rather than a clear, kind no.
